recordings.title: Booking a Coastal Bike Ride
recordings.context: مكالمة حجز رحلة دراجات على الساحل. اكتب بيانات الحجز في النموذج.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning, Coastal Cycle Tours, Priya speaking. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hi there. I'd like to book a place on your guided coastal ride, please. I saw the advert at the tourist office.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you for calling. Before we start, I should mention that all our rides are weather permitting, and if we have to cancel because of strong winds, we will offer you a new date or a full refund.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Of course. Which date were you thinking of?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: We were hoping to go on the twelfth of June, if there's space.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I'm afraid the twelfth is fully booked. We do have the 14th June, which is a Saturday, and then the 21st.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The 14th would be perfect, thanks.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Lovely. And how many people will be in your group?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: There'll be three of us... actually, no, my sister has just said she'd like to come too, so make that four.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Four adults, then. Can I take a name for the booking?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, it's Daniel Hartley.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Could you spell the surname for me?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sure. That's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you, Mr Hartley. And a contact number, please?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Let me read that back. 0 7 9 1 1, 4 6 2, 3 8 0. Is that right?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, that's it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great. The ride starts at 9 o'clock. Sorry, I should say 9.30 this month, because we've moved it to fit in with the tides.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's no problem. Where do we meet?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Outside the Lighthouse Café on the harbour front. The website still says the harbour car park, but that's out of date.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, the Lighthouse Café. And how much is it per person?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's £30 for the standard ride in spring, but from June the price goes up to £35 per person.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's fine. Do you have electric bikes? Two of us would prefer those, because of the hills.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, we do. Electric bikes are £10 extra each, so I'll note down two electric bikes for you. Everyone gets a helmet, and a packed lunch is included. Does anybody have any special dietary needs?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: One of us is vegetarian. Nobody has any allergies, though.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Perfect, one vegetarian lunch. Now, could I take an address and a postcode so that we can send you the confirmation?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, it's Flat 3, 18 Bramley Road, Leeds. The postcode is L-S-6, 2-Q-T.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you. I'll send everything this afternoon. There's a deposit of £20 per person, which you can pay online when you receive the confirmation.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Brilliant, I'll do that today. Thanks very much for your help, Priya.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You're welcome, Mr Hartley. We look forward to seeing you on the 14th. Have a lovely day.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: One last thing: please arrive ten minutes early so that we can fit your helmets, and bring a bottle of water and some sun cream.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Will do. Goodbye.

recordings.title: Hiring a Village Hall
recordings.context: مكالمة لحجز قاعة لحفلة. اكتب البيانات الناقصة في نموذج الحجز.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Hello, Elmwood Village Hall, Tom speaking.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Oh, hello. I'm hoping to hire a room for a family party. Is that something you can help with?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Absolutely. Let me take a few details first. What kind of event is it?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's a wedding anniversary. My parents have been married for forty years, and my brother and I want to surprise them.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: How lovely. Congratulations to them. We host quite a few anniversary parties, so I know what you'll need. Is it going to be a sit-down meal or a buffet?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A buffet, I think. We'll organise the food ourselves.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's fine. You can use our kitchen at no extra charge, but please leave it clean. Which date did you have in mind?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I was thinking of the 22nd August, but my brother can't make it that weekend, so it'll be the 23rd August instead.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Let me check the diary. Yes, the 23rd August is free. And roughly how many guests are you expecting?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: About fifty, I think. Well, once we add all the cousins, it'll be nearer sixty.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Then the Willow Room won't be big enough, because it only holds forty. You'd need the Oak Room, which takes up to eighty people.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The Oak Room sounds perfect. What does it cost?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's £45 an hour. It was £40 last year, but the committee put the price up in January. There's a deposit of £100, which is returned if there's no damage.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's fine. We'd like to start the party at 6.30 pm and finish at about 11. Is that possible?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We can't go beyond 11 pm because of the noise rules, but that gives you plenty of time. You can have the room from 5.30 to set up, though you'd be paying for that extra hour.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Oh, we'll manage with the 6.30 start. Do you have any equipment we could use? I'd like to show a slideshow of old family photographs.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, we have a projector and a screen, and they're free for hirers. There's also a small sound system, but there's a charge of £10 for that.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Just the projector, then. Thank you.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No problem. Now, could I take a name for the booking?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Fiona Mackenzie.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Could you spell your surname for me, please?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Of course. It's M-A-C-K-E-N-Z-I-E.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thanks, Fiona. And a phone number in case we need to contact you?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Got it. I'll post a booking form to you today, and I'll need it back with the deposit within two weeks. Otherwise, we may have to release the date.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'll do it as soon as it arrives. Thank you so much, Tom.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: My pleasure. I hope your parents enjoy the party. Goodbye.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Goodbye.

recordings.title: A Tour of Parkside Community Centre
recordings.context: جولة تعريفية داخل مركز مجتمعي. استخدم وصف الخريطة لتحديد أماكن الغرف، ثم أجب عن أسئلة المعلومات.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Parkside Community Centre. My name's Helen, and I'm going to show you around the ground floor before telling you a little about how the centre works.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We'll start at the main entrance, where we are now. As you can see, there's a long corridor that runs straight ahead of you to the main hall at the far end. All the rooms I'll mention are either off this corridor or at the end of it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Reception is the first door on your left as you come in. That's where you sign in, collect your membership card and ask any questions. Directly opposite reception, on the right, is our little shop, which sells stationery, sports socks and a few snacks.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Moving a bit further down the corridor, the next door on the left is the computer room. It has twelve machines and is used for evening classes as well as for free public sessions. You'll find the café on the opposite side, facing the computer room. People often think it's still next to the shop, because that's where it used to be, but it moved last spring when we put in the new kitchen.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: At the far end of the left-hand side, in the corner, is the craft studio. It's a bright room with big windows, which is why we chose it for painting and pottery. On the other side of the corridor, in the opposite corner, is the gym. It's small but well equipped, and there's a changing room attached.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Straight ahead, at the end of the corridor, you'll find the main hall. It can seat two hundred people, and we use it for concerts, markets and theatre groups. Beyond it, a door leads out to a terrace where you can sit in good weather.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now, a few practical details. The centre is open from eight in the morning until ten at night on weekdays. Some of the old leaflets say seven, but we changed that in January. At weekends we open at nine and close at six.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Membership costs twenty-five pounds a year. It used to be fifteen, but the council reduced our funding, so we had to raise it. Anyone under eighteen pays half price, and there's a family ticket, too, at forty pounds.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Members can use the computer room free of charge, and they get ten per cent off in the café. The gym, however, is charged separately at three pounds a session, even for members.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: If you want to hire the main hall for a private event, please don't phone reception. You need to fill in the form on our website at least a month in advance, and the manager, Mr Dawson, will contact you.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Finally, this Saturday we have our annual open day. There will be free taster classes in pottery and yoga from ten o'clock until three. You don't need to book for pottery, but yoga places are limited to twenty, so you should reserve one at reception if you're interested.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you for listening. If you'd like to see any of the rooms more closely, please follow me.

recordings.title: Harbourside Food Festival Briefing
recordings.context: اجتماع تعريفي للمتطوعين وأصحاب الأكشاك قبل مهرجان طعام. ركّز على الأرقام والتعديلات.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming along to this briefing for volunteers and stallholders at the Harbourside Food Festival. I'm Craig, the festival coordinator, and I'd like to run through the main points before we get started.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: First, a little background. The festival began twelve years ago as a small market with just eight stalls. It was started by a group of local fishermen who wanted to raise money for the lifeboat station after its roof was damaged in a storm. Many people think it was set up to attract tourists, but that only became a goal later on.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It has grown a great deal since then. Last year we had about a hundred stalls, and this year there will be around a hundred and twenty, spread along the whole harbour front and into the old fish market. That's more food, more visitors and, of course, more work for all of us.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The festival runs from Thursday to Sunday. Gates open at ten each morning and close at six, except on Friday, when we're trying something new: a night market that stays open until ten, with live music. We've had children's cooking classes for years, so that's not the new feature this time.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now, getting there. Parking near the harbour is very limited, so please encourage visitors to leave their cars at the station car park. A shuttle bus runs from there to the harbour every ten minutes. Last year it ran every fifteen minutes, but visitors complained about the queues, so we've paid for an extra bus.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Tickets are eight pounds for adults at the gate, but if you buy online beforehand, the price is six pounds. Children under twelve go in free. Please tell your customers about the online discount, because it really does reduce the queues at the entrance.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The cooking demonstrations take place in the blue tent beside the lighthouse. The red tent is for children's activities, and the green tent is where drinks are sold. Please make sure visitors know the difference, because the printed programme still has the wrong colours in one place, and we don't want people to get lost.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We're also trying to cut down on plastic this year. Stallholders will not be allowed to hand out plastic bags, and we're asking visitors to bring their own reusable bottle. Water refill points will be available at three places along the harbour.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A word about the money. Profits from the festival are shared. Half goes to the lifeboat station, and the other half goes towards a new play area in the park. We'll announce the final figure on the festival website at the end of the month.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: If anyone loses something, it will be kept at the information office, which is next to the main gate. Please don't take items to the police station, as some volunteers did last year, because visitors then can't find them.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's everything from me. Does anybody have any questions?

recordings.title: Lecture: Green Roofs in Cities
recordings.context: محاضرة جامعية عن الأسطح الخضراء. أكمل الملاحظات بكلمة أو كلمتين على الأكثر. انتبه للتصحيحات.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about green roofs, which are roofs partly or completely covered with vegetation, and about why more and more cities are encouraging them.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Let me begin with a little history. Although green roofs seem modern, people have grown plants on roofs for centuries. In northern Europe, farmers covered their houses with turf, mainly for insulation, and some of these buildings in Iceland survive today. The modern version, however, was developed in Germany in the 1960s, and Germany has led the world in the technology ever since.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There are two main types. The first is the extensive roof, which has a thin layer of soil, usually only about ten centimetres... sorry, I mean about fifteen centimetres deep, and low-growing plants such as moss and sedum. These roofs are light, cheap and need very little maintenance, perhaps one visit a year. The second type is the intensive roof, which is more like a real garden. It can support shrubs and even small trees, but the soil is much deeper, so the building must be stronger, and the cost is considerably higher.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What are the benefits? The first is temperature. On a hot summer day, a conventional roof can reach seventy degrees Celsius, while a green roof stays close to the temperature of the air. This reduces the need for air conditioning inside the building. Studies suggest energy savings of up to twenty per cent for the top floor... no, I should correct that, up to fifteen per cent, since the twenty per cent figure came from a single experimental building.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The second benefit is water management. Plants and soil absorb rainwater, so less water runs into the drains during storms. A typical extensive roof can hold back around half of the rain that falls on it, which helps to prevent flooding in heavy rain.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Third, there is wildlife. Even small green roofs attract insects, birds and bees, and in some cities, rare species of spider and beetle have been recorded on rooftops. There are also social benefits, because roof gardens give office workers a place to relax, and research suggests that employees with views of greenery report lower stress.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Of course, there are drawbacks. The main one is cost. Installing a green roof costs roughly twice as much as a normal roof, mainly because a special waterproof layer must be installed first, to protect the building from roots. The second is weight. A saturated roof can weigh more than two hundred kilograms per square metre, so older buildings may need strengthening before anything is planted. And the third is maintenance. Although extensive roofs need little attention, weeds must be removed and the irrigation system must be checked regularly in dry summers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because of these costs, many governments use incentives. In Toronto, for example, the city requires green roofs on large new buildings. In other places, owners receive a discount on their water bill, because their roofs reduce the amount of rainwater that the drainage system has to handle.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: To sum up, green roofs are not suitable for every building, but they offer a range of benefits that justify their cost in many urban settings. For your assignment next week, I'd like you to compare the costs and benefits of one type of roof for a building of your choice and make a recommendation. Please submit it by Friday. Thank you, and see you next time.

recordings.title: Lecture: How Honeybees Communicate
recordings.context: محاضرة عن لغة الرقص عند النحل. أكمل الملاحظات بكلمة واحدة على الأكثر. لاحظ التصحيحات.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Today's lecture is about one of the most remarkable examples of animal communication: the dance language of honeybees. This was discovered by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who spent more than forty years studying bees, and who shared a Nobel Prize in 1973.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Von Frisch noticed that when a forager bee found a good source of nectar, she returned to the hive and performed a kind of dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, in the dark. Other bees crowded around her, and soon afterwards they flew directly to the same flowers. He set out to discover how this information was being passed on.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There are two main dances. The first is the round dance, which a bee performs when the food is close to the hive, within about a hundred metres... no, sorry, I mean fifty metres, according to the most careful measurements. This dance tells the others that food is nearby, but not in which direction. The second, more complex dance is the waggle dance, which is used for food that is farther away. The bee walks in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement in a pattern like a figure of eight.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The information in the waggle dance is encoded in two ways. Firstly, the direction of the straight run, measured against the vertical, shows the angle between the sun and the food. If the bee runs straight up the comb, the food lies in the direction of the sun. If she runs thirty degrees to the right of the vertical, the food lies thirty degrees to the right of the sun. Secondly, the distance is shown by the length of the waggle. As a rough guide, each second of waggling represents about one kilometre.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Since the hive is dark, how do the other bees read the dance? They touch the dancer's body with their antennae and feel the vibrations. Experiments with robot bees, built to copy the movements, have shown that the dancing alone is enough to send followers in the right direction.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Bees also adjust for the movement of the sun. As the day passes, the sun moves across the sky, so the dancer gradually changes the angle of her runs. Even on cloudy days, bees can find the position of the sun by detecting polarised light, which is invisible to us.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The quality of the food is communicated too. A bee that has found a rich source dances for longer and with more energy, so that more workers are recruited. Poor sources produce short, weak dances, and some bees simply stop dancing altogether.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not every scientist accepted von Frisch's theory at first. In the 1960s, critics argued that bees found food by smell alone, rather than by following dance instructions. Later, researchers used radar to follow individual bees from the hive, and the results supported von Frisch.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: More recent research has shown that bees also use the dance when a swarm has to find a new home. Scout bees dance to advertise different possible locations, and the swarm finally chooses the site that attracts the largest number of dancers. In other words, the colony makes a collective decision, without any single leader.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: For next week, please read the article on the reading list and prepare a short summary of the evidence for and against von Frisch's theory. We'll discuss it in the seminar. Thank you.
